name: Coal tar shampoo

lead: Coal tar shampoo is an over-the-counter medicated wash used to clear the flakes and scale of dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and scalp psoriasis, leaving a clearer scalp with fewer visible flakes. Coal tar is a dark by-product of coke and coal-gas production.

Tar is traditionally described as keratolytic and anti-inflammatory, slowing scalp skin turnover, though Wikipedia does not detail how it works. Controlled studies from 1980 to 2000 reported it effective in psoriasis, dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis, while a double-blind trial found a non-tar shampoo as effective as a 0.5% coal tar shampoo for dandruff.

paras: People use it as a medicated wash a few times a week, lathered on the scalp and left briefly before rinsing. Its strong smell and staining limit how many stick with it.

Irritation, folliculitis, phototoxicity and contact dermatitis are reported. Coal tars are IARC Group 1 carcinogens, and a mid-1990s Lancet correspondence debated carcinogenic potential and measured skin uptake after hair washing. Wikipedia reports the EU forbade coal tar in cosmetics in 2009.

angle.text: Coal tar shampoo slows scalp skin turnover to clear flaking and scaling from dandruff and scalp psoriasis, so the scalp looks clearer. Controlled studies reported it effective; its odor and staining limit acceptance.

lead: Coal tar shampoo is a medicated shampoo containing coal tar, a viscous dark by-product of coke and coal-gas production, sold over the counter for dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and scalp psoriasis.[1] Wikipedia notes that patient acceptance is limited because tar products can stain, smell strongly and be messy.[1]

Controlled studies from 1980 to 2000 reported it effective in psoriasis, dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis, while a double-blind trial found a non-tar shampoo was as effective as a 0.5% coal tar shampoo for dandruff.[2][3] Coal tars are classified by the IARC as Group 1 carcinogens, and a mid-1990s correspondence in The Lancet debated the carcinogenic potential of coal tar shampoo and measured skin uptake of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons after hair washing.[1][4][5][6]
infobox: Coal tar forbidden in cosmetics by a 2009 directive (per Wikipedia)

paras: Coal tar is used topically for dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and psoriasis and is sold as shampoo, gel, cream or ointment for external use.[1] Brand names listed on Wikipedia include Balnetar and Cutar.[1]

Reported side effects include irritation, folliculitis, contact dermatitis, phototoxicity and pigmentation changes; coal tar is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency and, per Wikipedia, topical use raises concern about skin cancer because many constituents are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.[1] The IARC lists coal tars as Group 1 carcinogens, and Wikipedia states a 2009 EU directive forbade coal tar in cosmetics.[1]

Research on shampoo specifically includes a 1980 Salmonella/liver test that found differing degrees of mutagenesis among coal tar shampoos, a 1994 Lancet study of dermal uptake of PAHs after washing with coal-tar shampoo, and 1995 Lancet letters on its carcinogenicity.[4][5][6][7]
A 1980 clinical re-evaluation of an alkaline whole coal tar shampoo reported efficacy in psoriasis, dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and pruritus, along with cosmetic hair-condition improvements.[2]

In a randomized double-blind study of 60 volunteers with moderate to marked dandruff, a non-tar shampoo (salicylic acid, piroctone olamine and elubiol) was compared with a 0.5% coal tar shampoo; investigators reported the non-tar product was as effective.[3]
A registered study (NCT05105139) examined safety of other shampoos in seborrheic dermatitis and scalp psoriasis.[8]
